newsitem.title: USA: Atlanta remembers Olympic bombing one year later.
newsitem.headline: Atlanta remembers Olympic bombing one year later.

text.p: A candlelight ceremony and a memorial service marked the first anniversary on Sunday of the bombing in Centennial Olympic Park that led to two deaths and injured 111 others during last summer's Olympic Games.

A California man who was in the park when the bomb exploded placed candles in the shape of a 30-foot peace symbol at 1:20 a.m. (5:20 GMT) Sunday morning, the exact time when the bomb in a military backpack exploded during a rock concert last year.
Ron Jones of Palo Alto, Calif., also put up signs in the park reading: "To the Olympic Park bomber, please surrender."
"The perpetrator always comes back to the scene of the crime," Jones told Reuters. He said he did not want the victims of last year's blast to be forgotten.
"The community needs to do something, but no one around here seems to want to do anything. They seem to want to forget it," Jones said.

Later in the day, Atlanta Mayor Bill Campbell led a short prayer and laid a wreath in memory of Alice Hawthorne, an Albany, Ga., woman who was killed while in the park celebrating her daughter's 14th birthday. The other death from the bombing was that of a Turkish television cameraman who died of a heart attack running to the scene.
Fallon Stubbs, who suffered shrapnel wounds in the bombing that killed her mother, said she does not hold out hope that the person who planted the bomb will be caught.
"When I see it on TV, anything about the Olympic bombing, it just really gets to me," Stubbs said. "I just hope they know within themselves that they did it and that that will eat them up inside."

Federal investigators have narrowed down to about 10 minutes the period during which someone placed the 40-pound pipe bomb under a bench in the park. But they have identified no suspects since security guard Richard Jewell was named in press reports three days after the bombing.

Jewell won undisclosed damages from NBC and CNN because of reports identifying him as the suspect before he was cleared by investigators 88 days later. Lawsuits are pending against the Atlanta Journal-Constitution and the New York Post.
In an interview with an Atlanta television station on Sunday, Jewell said the money from out-of-court settlements is small consolation for what he called "88 days of hell."

"Walk an hour in my shoes during that time," Jewell told WXIA-TV. "My career has been ruined. I haven't been able to find a job in my chosen career, which is law enforcement. I love public safety and service and I'm still trying to get a job. I'm still unemployed."
A year after the bombing, parts of Centennial Olympic Park, including the spot where the bomb went off, are still closed to the public for renovations.

FBI agent Jack Daulton, who heads the bombing investigation, said there was a "strong possibility" that the Olympic bombing was linked to bombings early this year at an abortion clinic and a gay nightclub.
